Science communication · bees and plants of California

Do California's bee hotspots match its plant hotspots? · 2026-11-22

A plain-language guide to “Patterns of species richness and endemism in bee and plant communities in California” (Alarcon-Cruz et al. 2026, iScience 29, 118217) · 559,021 museum specimens of 1,742 native bee species and 1,333,270 flowering-plant records, mapped on 1,694 15-km squares: where bee species are most numerous, where the rarest bees live, and how both line up with flowering plants.

By Gretchen LeBuhn, UCSB · 2026-11-22 08:37 PST

Native bees pollinate California's wildflowers and many of its crops, yet until now no one had mapped where they are found across the state. This study is that first statewide map, built from 559,021 museum specimens of 1,742 native bee species. It shows where the most species of bees are found, and where the rare bees are concentrated. These rare bees are range-restricted (endemic) in the way that matters for policy: their whole range covers only a few places, so losing those places could mean losing the species. Many of them live in working and dry landscapes: the San Joaquin Valley, east of the Sierra Nevada, the Sierra foothills and the deserts. In the San Joaquin Valley, rare-bee hot spots sit in one of the nation's most important food-producing regions, where wetlands, grasslands and woodlands have been converted to farmland, groundwater is being drawn down, soils are growing saltier and pesticide use has increased.

Conservation plans are usually built on plant data, and because bees feed on flowers, you might expect protecting the richest plant areas to protect bees too. The map shows it does not. Plant diversity explains only 22% of the differences in how many kinds of bees an area has, and less than 1% of where the rare bees are. The plant hot spots of the wet northwest and the High Sierra have few bee hot spots, while many rare-bee hot spots lie in the deserts and the San Joaquin Valley, where plant diversity is low. The paper gives reasons: about 30% of flowering plants are pollinated by wind, by themselves or by animals other than bees; plants differ greatly in how much pollen and nectar they offer; many bees are specialists that depend on a few plants and can persist where flowers are scarce; and bees need nesting sites and tend to be most diverse in drier climates, while plant diversity rises with rainfall. Planning for pollinators, on farmland and in protected areas, needs bee data, not plant data alone.

Where are California's bees most diverse, and where are the rarest?

Two different questions: how many kinds of bees live in a place (species richness), and how many of them live almost nowhere else (endemism).

Darker squares have more bee species on record, up to 399 in one square.

245 squares form hot spots for the number of bee species: the Bay Area and Central Coast, the South Coast Ranges, the central High Sierra and the mountains of southern California.

149 squares are hot spots for rare bees, smaller and more scattered: the San Joaquin Valley, east of the Sierra Nevada, the foothills and the deserts.

Collecting is uneven: half of the squares have 43 specimens or fewer, one has 43,478. 265 squares have plant records but no bee specimens at all.

How this panel was checked
  • Squares with no bee specimens are drawn white and called unknown, not bee-free.
  • The paper counts 1,694 squares with bee specimens. The hot spot analysis also includes one square in the east Mojave that is in the grid output without specimens, so hot spot counts and shares on this page are out of 1,695.
  • A hot spot is a cluster of high values, not a single high square; significance levels are as in the paper and not adjusted for testing many squares at once (stated in Figures 7–8).
  • The 'how well collected' view is shown next to the species maps because more specimens means more species found.

Bee diversity comes in broad regions; rare bees come in pockets

The number of species changes smoothly across the state. Rare-bee places are about 3 times less clustered: isolated squares with unusual bees, surrounded by ordinary ones.Moran's I richness 0.300 vs CWE 0.089 (ratio 3.4); both p < 0.0001.

Shared hot spots (158 squares) cluster in the mountains of southern California, along the High Sierra and around San Francisco Bay.

Shared rare-species hot spots are few (34 squares): mostly east of the Sierra Nevada and in the White and Inyo Mountains, with smaller groups on the Modoc Plateau and near Death Valley.

How this panel was checked
  • The bee and plant analyses use the same grid and the same hot spot method, so each square is compared like for like.
  • Plant data come from older herbarium collections (to 2017) and were collected more evenly than bees; agreement could partly reflect where people collected, as the paper notes.
  • Classes are those of the paper's Figure 10; colours keep bees in vermillion and plants in green throughout this page.

Plants predict bee species counts only partly, and rare bees hardly at all

Squares with more kinds of flowering plants tend to have more kinds of bees, but plants explain only 21.5% of the differences between squares. For rare species they explain less than 1%: knowing where rare plants are tells you almost nothing about where rare bees are.Linear regressions at cell level (n = 1,694): richness R² = 0.215; CWE R² = 0.0078 (F = 13.39, p = 0.0003).

How this panel was checked
  • Each dot is one square; both groups are counted in the same squares.
  • Bee species counts rise with collecting effort (see 'Behind the numbers'), which adds scatter to this comparison.
  • Rare-species scores are drawn on log scales because a few squares are far higher than the rest; no line is drawn because the fit explains under 1%.

Where would plant-based conservation miss bees?

Hot spots for bees that are not hot spots for plants are places a plants-only plan would leave out.

Bee hot spots that plant-based planning would miss, by region

115 squares are hot spots for rare bees but not for rare plants, and 87 are hot spots for bee species but not plant species. Behind the numbers

The key methods choice: museum collections are uneven, so the paper measures rarity in a way that does not simply reward well-collected places.

From 3.0 million records to 559,021 specimens

Most records were dropped because they were outside California or were observations rather than museum specimens. Duplicates (the same specimen listed in two databases) and non-native bees were removed too.Table S1 attrition; steps 5 and 9 removed no records and are omitted.

Why the paper measures rarity with a corrected score

Collect more bees in a square and you find more species: effort alone explains 87% of the differences in species counts (left). So the paper scores rarity with corrected weighted endemism: each bee counts more the fewer squares it lives in (a bee found in one square counts 1, one found in 100 squares counts 0.01), and the score is the average over the species present. That average barely depends on effort (13%, right), so rare-bee hot spots are less likely to be just well-collected places.Log–log OLS of cell values on n occurrences (n = 1,694): richness slope 0.656, R² 0.870; CWE slope 0.170, R² 0.132. CWE = WE / richness, WE = Σ 1/range (range in occupied cells).

How this panel was checked
  • Both panels use the same squares and the same specimen counts.
  • Log scales on both axes, because specimen counts run from 1 to tens of thousands.
  • The paper uses observed species counts; it reports that an estimate of missed species (Chao1) ranks squares much the same way (Table S7).
